title: Randomized: Reservoir Sampling
oneLiner: Keep a fair random sample of k items from a stream you can only read once and whose length you don't know: item i replaces a random slot with probability k / (i + 1).
keyTakeaway: Fill the reservoir with the first k items. For each later item at index i, draw j uniformly from 0 to i; if j < k, the item replaces reservoir[j], otherwise it is dropped. Every item seen so far ends up in the sample with the same probability k / (i + 1), using O(k) memory and one pass.
explanation:
Items arrive one by one from a stream too large to store, maybe of unknown length. Keep a sample of k of them such that, at the end, every item had the same chance to be in it. As in Fisher-Yates Shuffle, randomness can't be graded, so the draws are given: draws[i] is the random integer from 0 to i that the generator returned for the item at index i (the values for i < k are not used). Return the reservoir after the whole stream.

Algorithm R: put stream[0..k - 1] straight into the reservoir. For each later index i, let j = draws[i] (in real code, rng.Next(i + 1)). If j < k, replace reservoir[j] with stream[i]; otherwise skip the item. For [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], k = 2 and draws [0, 0, 1, 3, 0]: start [10, 20]; 30 draws 1 and replaces 20; 40 draws 3, which is not below 2, so it is skipped; 50 draws 0 and replaces 10. Result [50, 30].

Why it is fair: item i enters with probability k / (i + 1). Later item m (m > i) then evicts that particular slot with probability 1 / (m + 1), so item i survives it with probability m / (m + 1). Multiplying from i + 1 to n - 1 telescopes: (k / (i + 1)) · ((i + 1) / (i + 2)) · ... · ((n - 1) / n) = k / n, the same for every item. The first k items work out to k / n as well.

One pass, O(1) work per item: O(n) time and O(k) space, and you can stop at any moment with a valid sample of what has been seen so far. Monitoring and logging systems use it to keep a representative handful of examples, and it is the answer to "pick a random node from a linked list of unknown length" (k = 1: replace the choice with probability 1 / (i + 1)).

The visualization runs the example above.

starterCode.python:
def reservoir_sample(stream, k, draws):
    reservoir = list(stream[:k])

    return reservoir

visualizationSteps.message: k = 2: the first two items, 10 and 20, fill the reservoir.
Item 30 (index 2) draws 1 from 0 to 2. 1 < 2, so it replaces 20 in slot 1. It got in with probability 2/3.
Item 40 (index 3) draws 3 from 0 to 3. 3 is not below 2, so it is skipped.
Item 50 (index 4) draws 0 from 0 to 4. 0 < 2, so it replaces 10 in slot 0. It got in with probability 2/5.
Stream finished: sample [50, 30]. Every item had probability 2/5 of ending up here.

recognitionSignals: A random sample from a stream, a huge file or a linked list, in one pass and without knowing the length.
"Each item must be chosen with equal probability" and you can't store everything.
gotchas: Keeping item i with probability k / n needs n in advance; the point of the algorithm is k / (i + 1), using only what you have seen.
Draw j from 0 to i inclusive; 0 to i - 1 makes the newest item too likely.
If the stream has fewer than k items, the reservoir is simply all of them.
confusableWith: Fisher-Yates Shuffle needs the whole array in memory; reservoir sampling never stores more than k items.
Top K with a Heap also keeps k items from a stream, but chooses them by value, not at random.

complexity.note: One pass over the n items with O(1) work each. Only the k-slot reservoir is stored, however long the stream.
